title: GC: Reference Counting + Generational Cyclic Garbage Collector

progressiveExplaining.eli5: Every Python object has a counter on its back showing how many people are pointing at it. When the counter hits zero, it is instantly thrown in the trash. But if Object A points to Object B, and Object B points back to Object A, their counters never hit zero even if the rest of the world forgets them. A special garbage detective (the Cyclic GC) periodically walks the memory, finds these isolated circles, and deletes them.
progressiveExplaining.junior: CPython's primary memory management is **Reference Counting** (`ob_refcnt`). When an object's reference count reaches `0`, it is deallocated immediately and synchronously. To solve **Cyclic References** (where Object A references B and B references A, keeping `refcnt >= 1` forever), CPython has a secondary **Generational Cyclic Garbage Collector** (`gc` module) with 3 generations (Gen 0, Gen 1, Gen 2).
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Reference Counting is deterministic: destructors (`__del__`) and context manager cleanups run immediately when references drop to zero. The Cyclic GC is an asynchronous stop-the-world tracing collector that runs only on container objects (`list`, `dict`, `set`, custom class instances) that can hold references to other objects. It tracks doubly-linked lists of `PyGC_Head` headers. Generation 0 collections run frequently based on allocation thresholds; surviving objects are promoted to Generation 1 and eventually Generation 2.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: Container objects allocate a `PyGC_Head` header immediately before the `PyObject` structure. The cyclic collection algorithm works by copying `ob_refcnt` to a temporary `gc_refs` field in the GC list. It iterates through all pointers in the candidate set using `tp_traverse`, decrementing `gc_refs` on referenced objects. If an object's `gc_refs` drops to `0`, it can only be reached through internal cyclic references within the candidate group and is marked unreachable and freed.

rosettaStone.python: Reference Counting (immediate) + Generational Cyclic GC (3 generations).
rosettaStone.go: Tri-color Mark-Sweep concurrent collector (no reference counting).
rosettaStone.java: Generational G1 / ZGC tracing collectors (no reference counting).

codeComparison.title: Immediate Reference Count Deallocation vs Cyclic Reference Leak
codeComparison.summary: Linear references die immediately on scope exit; cyclic references stay in memory until the cyclic GC runs.

legacyOrBad.label: Cyclic Reference (Requires Tracing GC)
legacyOrBad.snippet: nodeA.other = nodeB; nodeB.other = nodeA; del nodeA, nodeB; // ❌ refcnt stays 1, requires GC cycle

fullFile.code:
import gc

class Node:
  def __init__(self, name):
    self.name = name
    self.other = None

# ❌ Creating a cyclic graph:
a = Node('A')
b = Node('B')
a.other = b
b.other = a

# Dropping global variables:
del a
del b
# a and b are NOT freed here! Both have refcnt = 1 because they point to each other.
# They will remain in memory until gc.collect() runs.

modernOrGood.label: Weak References (Zero-Cycle Reference Counting)
modernOrGood.snippet: import weakref; nodeB.other = weakref.ref(nodeA); // ✅ NEW: Instant refcnt=0 deallocation

fullFile.code:
import weakref

class Node:
  def __init__(self, name):
    self.name = name
    self.other = None

# ✅ NEW: Use weakref to break cyclic reference graphs
a = Node('A')
b = Node('B')
a.other = b
b.other = weakref.ref(a) # Weak reference does not increment ob_refcnt!

del a
# a is deallocated IMMEDIATELY and synchronously because its refcnt hit 0!
print('Is a alive?', b.other() is not None) # False

interviewGotchas.question: Why did `__del__` methods historically prevent CPython's cyclic GC from collecting cycles (pre-Python 3.4 / PEP 442)?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your historical knowledge of CPython's finalization mechanics.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Prior to Python 3.4, if two cyclic objects both defined a `__del__` destructor, Python had no safe way to determine which destructor should execute first without passing a half-destroyed object to the other. Consequently, CPython threw the cycle into `gc.garbage` and **leaked the memory forever**. In Python 3.4+ (PEP 442), Python modernized finalization: it breaks the cycle before calling `__del__`, allowing cyclic objects with destructors to be safely collected.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Even in modern Python, relying on `__del__` for critical cleanup is an anti-pattern; always use Context Managers (`with` blocks).

interviewGotchas.question: Can you disable the cyclic garbage collector in Python with `gc.disable()`, and what happens if you do?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Checks performance tuning and high-throughput production optimization skills.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Yes. Calling `gc.disable()` **disables the generational cyclic collector, but Reference Counting continues to function 100% normally**. 99% of non-cyclic objects are still deallocated immediately when their reference count reaches 0. High-scale services (like Instagram/Instagram Web) disable the cyclic GC to prevent GC pause latency during peak traffic, manually invoking `gc.collect()` during idle periods.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: `gc.disable()` will cause cyclic graphs to leak permanently unless broken manually via `weakref` or periodic manual `gc.collect()`.
